etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “father of a gift” or “my father is Jesse.”
biblical_def: Abishai was the son of Zeruiah, David’s sister, and the brother of Joab and Asahel—one of the fierce house of warriors who stood about David through his wilderness years and his reign. He was chief among a band of mighty men, of whom it is written that he lifted up his spear against three hundred and slew them, and had a name among the three. His courage was unflinching and his loyalty to David firm, yet his zeal often ran hot and bloody. When David crept into Saul’s camp by night, it was Abishai who went down with him and begged leave to smite the LORD’s anointed to the earth with one stroke; David restrained him, refusing to stretch out his hand against Saul. Again, when Shimei cursed the king, Abishai would have taken off the dead dog’s head, and again David held him back. He delivered David from the giant Ishbi-benob in battle, and he led troops against Edom and Ammon. In Abishai the Reformed reader sees real valor wedded to a spirit too quick for vengeance—a man whom God used mightily, yet whom mercy had to bridle. His life teaches that bravery without restraint is a sword that wounds friend and foe alike, and that the fear of the LORD, not the heat of the moment, must govern the strong.
webster_summary: A son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab; one of David’s foremost mighty men, valiant but hot for vengeance.
webster_full: ABISHAI, the son of Zeruiah, David’s sister, and brother of Joab and Asahel.
He was chief of the mighty men and had a name among the three, having slain three hundred with his spear (2Sa 23:18).
He went down with David into Saul’s camp and offered to smite the king, but was forbidden (1Sa 26:8).
He would have taken off Shimei’s head for cursing David, yet the king restrained him.
He succoured David against the giant in battle and warred against Edom and Ammon.
scriptures: Then said Abishai to David, God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day: now therefore let me smite him, I pray thee, with the spear even to the earth at once, and I will not smite him the second time.
And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD’S anointed, and be guiltless?
And Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief among three. And he lifted up his spear against three hundred, and slew them, and had the name among three.

But Abishai the son of Zeruiah succoured him, and smote the Philistine, and killed him. Then the men of David sware unto him, saying, Thou shalt go no more out with us to battle, that thou quench not the light of Israel.
corruption_summary: Abishai’s valor is honorable, yet his readiness for vengeance is the warning the narrative itself sounds.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is that courage and loyalty, however genuine, are not enough without the governing fear of the LORD. Twice Abishai stood ready to shed blood—against Saul and against Shimei—and twice David checked him, refusing to avenge himself and committing judgment to God. The strong man must learn that vengeance belongs to the LORD, who will repay.

Abishai’s life rebukes the modern instinct to admire raw boldness apart from holiness. He was mighty, but it was David’s restraint, not Abishai’s spear, that honored God in those hours. Real strength under grace knows when to sheathe the sword and wait upon the LORD’s righteous judgment.
roots_summary: The name binds Abishai to the house of Jesse and to the giving of a son’s strength to his father’s cause.
roots_lines: Abishai — Hebrew Avishai, “father of a gift” or “my father is Jesse.”
The element av (“father”) opens many Hebrew names of the period.
His mother Zeruiah is named oftener than his father, marking the renown of her sons.
The sons of Zeruiah—Joab, Abishai, Asahel—form a warrior triad about David.
His name endures among the lists of David’s mighty men in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles.
usage: Like Abishai, the bold servant must let his zeal be bridled by his master’s wisdom.
David trusted Abishai in battle, yet would not loose him for private revenge.
The valor of Abishai shielded the light of Israel when the king grew faint.

etymology: From the Hebrew, perhaps “burden” or “a people spared.”
biblical_def: Amasa was a kinsman of David, the son of his sister Abigail by Jether the Ishmeelite, and thus cousin to Joab. He rose to prominence as captain of the host under Absalom in the great rebellion against David. When that revolt was crushed and Amasa lay among the defeated, David—seeking to win Judah and to break the proud dominance of Joab—swore to make Amasa captain of the host in Joab’s room continually. Thus a man who had borne the sword against the king was set over the king’s armies, a striking display of David’s mercy and policy together. But Amasa proved slow to gather Judah within the appointed days, and in the pursuit of Sheba the son of Bichri, Joab met him at the great stone in Gibeon. Feigning a kinsman’s greeting, Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand as if to kiss him, and with the sword in his other hand smote him in the fifth rib, shedding out his bowels to the ground. So Amasa died in his own blood in the highway, a victim of Joab’s jealous treachery. His brief and bloody career shows how the throne’s favor cannot shield a man from the murderous ambition of the wicked, and how God’s providence threads even kingly mercy and base betrayal toward His own ends.
webster_summary: Absalom’s captain, later made David’s commander, slain treacherously by Joab at the stone in Gibeon.
webster_full: AMASA, the son of Abigail, David’s sister, by Jether the Ishmeelite, and cousin to Joab.
He was made captain of the host by Absalom in his rebellion against David (2Sa 17:25).
After the revolt David swore to set him over the army in Joab’s room.
He tarried longer than the set time in gathering the men of Judah.
Joab feigned a greeting and slew him in the fifth rib at the great stone in Gibeon (2Sa 20:10).
scriptures: And Absalom made Amasa captain of the host instead of Joab: which Amasa was a man’s son, whose name was Ithra an Israelite, that went in to Abigail the daughter of Nahash, sister to Zeruiah Joab’s mother.
And say ye to Amasa, Art thou not of my bone, and of my flesh? God do so to me, and more also, if thou be not captain of the host before me continually in the room of Joab.
And Joab said to Amasa, Art thou in health, my brother? And Joab took Amasa by the beard with the right hand to kiss him.

But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab’s hand: so he smote him therewith in the fifth rib, and shed out his bowels to the ground, and struck him not again; and he died. So Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri.
corruption_summary: Amasa’s end exposes the murderous jealousy that festers when men love power above the king’s peace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the deadliness of ambition that wears the mask of friendship. Joab’s kiss of greeting concealed the dagger of envy; he could not bear to be supplanted, and so he murdered his own kinsman in cold blood. The treachery is named treachery, and the blood of Amasa cried against Joab to David’s last charge.

Amasa also stands as a sober figure of misplaced trust—he took no heed to the sword. The believer is warned to discern the wolf beneath the warm word, and rulers are warned that mercy extended to former rebels must reckon with the jealousy of entrenched men. God’s providence governed even this, yet Joab bore the guilt.
roots_summary: The name may carry the sense of a burden borne or a people spared, fitting one caught between rebellion and royal favor.
roots_lines: Amasa — Hebrew, possibly from a root meaning “to bear a burden.”
His father is named both Jether and Ithra, an Ishmeelite or Israelite, in the records.
His mother Abigail was sister to David and to Zeruiah, mother of Joab.
Thus Amasa and Joab were cousins, rivals for the captaincy of the host.
His death at Gibeon is one of three murders David charged against Joab.
usage: Amasa took no heed to the sword—a warning against trusting the false embrace of an envious man.
Like Amasa, the latecomer to duty may find his delay turned to his ruin.
David’s charge concerning the blood of Amasa pursued Joab to his own end.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “the LORD is my master” or “my Lord is Jehovah.”
biblical_def: Adonijah was the fourth son of David, born of Haggith at Hebron, a very goodly man whom his father had not displeased at any time. As David grew old, Adonijah exalted himself, saying, I will be king; and he prepared chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run before him. He conferred with Joab the captain and Abiathar the priest, and made a great feast at the stone of Zoheleth, slaying sheep and oxen, that he might be proclaimed king while his father yet lived. But he called not Nathan the prophet, nor Benaiah, nor Solomon his brother, for he knew the throne was promised elsewhere. Nathan and Bathsheba moved swiftly; David rose and commanded that Solomon be anointed king and set upon the royal mule, and the people rejoiced so that the earth rent with the sound. Hearing it, Adonijah’s guests fled in fear, and he himself caught hold of the horns of the altar, begging mercy; Solomon spared him for that day. Yet afterward Adonijah sought Abishag the Shunammite to wife—a claim upon the late king’s harem and so upon the kingdom—and Solomon, discerning the renewed grasping for the crown, sent Benaiah, who fell upon him that he died. His name, “the LORD is my master,” stood in bitter contradiction to a heart that would master the kingdom by self-exaltation.
webster_summary: David’s fourth son, who exalted himself to be king and was at last put to death under Solomon for grasping again at the throne.
webster_full: ADONIJAH, the son of David by Haggith, born in Hebron.
He exalted himself, saying he would be king, with chariots and runners before him (1Ki 1:5).
He conspired with Joab and Abiathar and feasted at the stone of Zoheleth.
When Solomon was anointed he fled and caught the horns of the altar for refuge.
Seeking Abishag to wife, he was put to death by Benaiah at Solomon’s command (1Ki 2:25).
scriptures: Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king: and he prepared him chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.
And Adonijah feared because of Solomon, and arose, and went, and caught hold on the horns of the altar.
Then king Solomon sware by the LORD, saying, God do so to me, and more also, if Adonijah have not spoken this word against his own life.
And king Solomon sent by the hand of Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he fell upon him that he died.
corruption_summary: Adonijah is the perpetual portrait of self-exaltation that grasps at a throne God has not given.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the ruin of the man who exalts himself rather than waiting to be exalted by God. “I will be king” was his sentence of death; he prepared his pomp and feast while presuming upon a crown the LORD had appointed to Solomon. Self-promotion against the revealed will of God is rebellion, however goodly the man.

Adonijah’s clutching of the altar shows that even the forms of refuge cannot shelter an unrepentant heart that means to keep grasping. His later suit for Abishag was no innocent request but a covert reach for the kingdom, and Solomon rightly judged it. The presumptuous shall not stand; he that humbleth himself shall be exalted, but he that exalteth himself shall be abased.
roots_summary: His name confesses the LORD as master, even while his life sought to master the kingdom.
roots_lines: Adonijah — Hebrew Adoniyyah, “the LORD is my master.”
The element adon means “lord” or “master.”
The element yah is the shortened covenant name of Jehovah.
He was born fourth, after Amnon, Chileab, and Absalom, in Hebron.
His self-exaltation forms the dramatic hinge that opens the reign of Solomon.
usage: Like Adonijah, the man who says “I will be king” courts his own destruction.
Adonijah caught the horns of the altar, but no altar shelters a heart still set on rebellion.
His suit for Abishag unmasked the same ambition that had feasted at Zoheleth.

etymology: From the Hebrew, perhaps meaning “plant” or “a statue.”
biblical_def: Ziba was a servant of the house of Saul, a man with fifteen sons and twenty servants of his own. When David sought to show the kindness of God to any that remained of Saul’s house for Jonathan’s sake, Ziba was summoned and disclosed that Jonathan had a son yet living, Mephibosheth, lame in his feet. David restored to Mephibosheth all the land of Saul and appointed Ziba and his household to till it, that the king’s table might feed his master’s son. Thus far Ziba served faithfully. But when Absalom’s rebellion drove David from Jerusalem, Ziba met the fleeing king with asses laden and provision—and with a slander. He charged that Mephibosheth had stayed behind hoping to seize the kingdom of his fathers, and David, in haste, granted Ziba all that was Mephibosheth’s. Yet when David returned in peace, Mephibosheth came mourning, unwashed and unkempt since the king departed, and protested that Ziba had deceived him, leaving him no beast to ride. David, unable to sift the matter, divided the land between them; and Mephibosheth, in love for the king, said, Let him take all. Ziba stands as a portrait of the opportunist—a servant who served while it profited him, then bore false witness to advance himself in a day of his master’s distress.
webster_summary: A servant of Saul’s house who served Mephibosheth, then slandered him to David to seize his inheritance.
webster_full: ZIBA, a servant of the house of Saul, having fifteen sons and twenty servants.
He revealed to David that Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth was yet living and lame (2Sa 9:3).
He was appointed to till Saul’s restored land for Mephibosheth’s sake.
In Absalom’s revolt he met fleeing David with gifts and slandered his master (2Sa 16:3).
David first gave him all Mephibosheth’s land, then divided it between them (2Sa 19:29).
scriptures: And the king said, Is there not yet any of the house of Saul, that I may shew the kindness of God unto him? And Ziba said unto the king, Jonathan hath yet a son, which is lame on his feet.
And the king said, And where is thy master’s son? And Ziba said unto the king, Behold, he abideth at Jerusalem: for he said, To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father.
Then said the king to Ziba, Behold, thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth. And Ziba said, I humbly beseech thee that I may find grace in thy sight, my lord, O king.
And the king said unto him, Why speakest thou any more of thy matters? I have said, Thou and Ziba divide the land.
corruption_summary: Ziba is the type of the self-serving slanderer who exploits a master’s extremity for his own gain.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the wickedness of bearing false witness against a defenceless man for profit. Ziba served Mephibosheth so long as the service paid; but in David’s day of flight he saw advantage and slandered the lame son of Jonathan, snatching at an inheritance that was not his. The eighth and ninth commandments alike are trodden under his ambition.

Ziba’s opportunism is set in sharp relief against Mephibosheth’s devotion, who cared nothing for the land so long as the king came home in peace. The contrast warns the believer: love that clings to the master is precious in God’s sight, while the calculating heart that profits by another’s ruin is loathsome, though it bring gifts in its hands.
roots_summary: The name is obscure, fitting a man known less for himself than for his treachery toward his master’s son.
roots_lines: Ziba — Hebrew Tsiva, of uncertain sense, perhaps “plant” or “statue.”
He is identified solely as a servant of the house of Saul.
His large household of sons and servants marks him a man of substance.
His name is linked always with Mephibosheth, whom he served and betrayed.
Scripture leaves the final verdict to the divided land and the king’s weary word.
usage: Like Ziba, the false servant gives gifts with one hand and slanders with the other.
Ziba met the fleeing king with provision, but his heart sought another’s inheritance.
Beware the Ziba who serves only while the serving profits him.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “brother of folly” or “my brother is foolishness.”
biblical_def: Ahithophel the Gilonite was David’s counselor, a man whose wisdom was so esteemed that his counsel in those days was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God; so was all his counsel both with David and with Absalom. Yet this trusted intimate, the king’s familiar friend who ate at his table, became the chief brain of Absalom’s rebellion. When the conspiracy was formed, Absalom sent for Ahithophel, and the conspiracy grew strong, for the people increased continually with Absalom. His counsel was deadly in its shrewdness: he urged Absalom to defile his father’s concubines openly upon the housetop, fulfilling Nathan’s prophecy of judgment, and he sought leave to pursue David at once with twelve thousand men while the king was weary and weak-handed, to smite him alone before he could rally. Had that counsel stood, David might have fallen. But David had prayed, O LORD, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness; and God answered through Hushai the Archite, whose rival counsel the LORD appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to bring evil upon Absalom. When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his ass, set his house in order, and hanged himself, and died—a dark foreshadowing of another betrayer of the Son of David. His name, “brother of folly,” sealed his end.
webster_summary: David’s counselor of oracular wisdom who betrayed him for Absalom, and hanged himself when his counsel was rejected.
webster_full: AHITHOPHEL, the Gilonite, counselor to David and the king’s familiar friend.
His counsel was esteemed as the oracle of God, both with David and Absalom (2Sa 16:23).
He joined Absalom’s conspiracy and counseled the open defiling of David’s house.
He sought to pursue and smite the weary David at once with twelve thousand men.
When his counsel was not followed he hanged himself and was buried in his father’s sepulchre (2Sa 17:23).
scriptures: And Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counsellor, from his city, even from Giloh, while he offered sacrifices. And the conspiracy was strong; for the people increased continually with Absalom.
And the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.

And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel. For the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom.

And when Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his ass, and arose, and gat him home to his house, to his city, and put his household in order, and hanged himself, and died, and was buried in the sepulchre of his father.
corruption_summary: Ahithophel is the byword of the trusted friend turned traitor, whose wisdom could not save him from despairing ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is that the keenest natural wisdom, severed from the fear of God, ends in folly and self-destruction. Ahithophel’s counsel was as the oracle of God, yet he turned it against the LORD’s anointed, and the LORD turned it into foolishness in answer to a single prayer. Man’s craftiness is no match for the counsel of heaven.

His suicide marks him as a type of Judas, the familiar friend who lifted up his heel against his master and went to his own place. The psalms David penned in those days—of the friend who ate his bread and betrayed him—reach forward to the betrayal of Christ. Ahithophel warns that gifts without grace, and intimacy without fidelity, end in the noose of despair.
roots_summary: The name itself pronounces the verdict: brother of folly, whatever his reputation for wisdom.
roots_lines: Ahithophel — Hebrew, “brother of folly” or “my brother is foolishness.”
The element ach means “brother.”
The element tophel carries the sense of folly or unsavory things.
He was of Giloh in the hill country of Judah, hence the Gilonite.
His end by hanging foreshadows the traitor of the New Testament.
usage: Like Ahithophel, a man may give counsel as the oracle of God and yet perish a traitor.
David’s prayer turned the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.
The despair of Ahithophel warns that worldly wisdom without grace ends in ruin.

biblical_def: Hushai the Archite was David’s friend, named in the records simply as the king’s companion. When Absalom’s rebellion broke and David fled Jerusalem weeping, Hushai met him at the top of the mount of Olives with his coat rent and earth upon his head, ready to share his master’s reproach. David, too old to take him in flight, sent him back on a holy errand: to return to the city, feign loyalty to Absalom, and so defeat the counsel of Ahithophel for David’s sake. Hushai obeyed. He came to Absalom crying, God save the king, and when challenged for forsaking his friend, answered with words crafted to allay suspicion. Then, when Ahithophel counseled the swift pursuit of David, Absalom called also for Hushai, who rose and overthrew the deadly plan with persuasive speech—urging delay, a great gathering of all Israel, and Absalom himself leading the host—counsel framed to buy David time to escape across Jordan. So it was that the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, and Hushai was His chosen instrument. Through Zadok and Abiathar’s sons Hushai sent warning to David, and the king was delivered. Hushai stands as the loyal friend whose faithful cunning, blessed of God, became the human means of preserving the anointed king and his throne.
webster_summary: The Archite, David’s faithful friend, who returned to Absalom’s court to defeat the counsel of Ahithophel.
webster_full: HUSHAI, the Archite, called the friend or companion of David.
He met the fleeing king on Olivet with rent coat and earth upon his head (2Sa 15:32).
David sent him back to feign loyalty and overthrow Ahithophel’s counsel.
He persuaded Absalom to reject Ahithophel’s swift pursuit of David (2Sa 17:7).
By his counsel and warning the LORD preserved David across Jordan.
scriptures: And it came to pass, that when David was come to the top of the mount, where he worshipped God, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his coat rent, and earth upon his head:
So Hushai David’s friend came into the city, and Absalom came into Jerusalem.
And Hushai said unto Absalom, The counsel that Ahithophel hath given is not good at this time.

And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel. For the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom.
corruption_summary: Hushai’s loyal stratagem shows God ruling the counsels of men to save His anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the sovereignty of God over the counsels of men, and the worth of a faithful friend. Where Ahithophel betrayed, Hushai stayed true; and the LORD appointed Hushai’s words to undo the traitor’s wisdom. David prayed, and Hushai was the answer; the means were ordinary, but the hand was God’s.

Hushai also models costly fidelity. He risked his life in the rebel’s court, bore the shame of seeming desertion, and labored secretly for the king’s good. Such friendship, that will share reproach and venture all for a master in his low estate, is precious; and it pictures the truer Friend who never forsakes His own. The believer is called to like steadfastness.
roots_summary: The name “quick” suits the man whose swift, well-timed counsel turned the day for David.
roots_lines: Hushai — Hebrew Chushai, “quick” or “hasting.”
He is styled the Archite, of the family or place of the Archi near Bethel.
He bears the honored title “David’s friend” or companion.
His name stands ever in contrast with that of Ahithophel the traitor.
His descendant Baanah served among Solomon’s officers in later days.
usage: Like Hushai, a faithful friend will bear reproach to serve his master in distress.
The counsel of Hushai, blessed of God, undid the wisdom of Ahithophel.
Hushai returned into peril that the LORD’s anointed might be preserved.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “palm coast” or “land of palms.”
biblical_def: Ithamar was the youngest of the four sons of Aaron by Elisheba, brother to Nadab, Abihu, and Eleazar. When the two eldest were struck down for offering strange fire, the priesthood passed on through the surviving brothers, Eleazar and Ithamar, who ministered before the LORD in the sight of Aaron their father. Ithamar bore particular charge in the service of the tabernacle: the sum of the tabernacle was reckoned by his hand, and under his oversight stood the Gershonites and the Merarites, who bare the boards, bars, pillars, sockets, and the heavy furniture of the sanctuary in their journeyings. He was thus a faithful steward of the structure and burdens of God’s house. In later generations the high priesthood for a season ran through his line in Eli and his sons, until that house was set aside for its wickedness and the office returned to the line of Eleazar in Zadok. When David ordered the courses of the priests, he divided them by lot, sixteen chief men of the house of Eleazar and eight of the house of Ithamar, ordering the service of the LORD’s house with even hand. Ithamar stands as a quiet figure of faithful priestly duty, his sons numbered among the appointed courses, a reminder that God preserves an ordered ministry through generations of obedient service.
webster_summary: Aaron’s youngest son, who ministered as priest and was head of one of the courses David ordained.
webster_full: ITHAMAR, the youngest son of Aaron by Elisheba, brother to Eleazar.
He ministered as priest with Eleazar after the death of Nadab and Abihu (Exo 6:23).
The charge of the Gershonites and Merarites in tabernacle service was under his hand (Num 4:28).
The sum of the tabernacle was counted by his oversight.
David appointed eight courses of priests of the house of Ithamar (1Ch 24:4).
scriptures: Exo 6:23
And Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Naashon, to wife; and she bare him Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
Num 4:28
This is the service of the families of the sons of Gershon in the tabernacle of the congregation: and their charge shall be under the hand of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest.
Lev 10:6

And Moses said unto Aaron, and unto Eleazar and unto Ithamar, his sons, Uncover not your heads, neither rend your clothes; lest ye die, and lest wrath come upon all the people: but let your brethren, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning which the LORD hath kindled.

And there were more chief men found of the sons of Eleazar than of the sons of Ithamar; and thus were they divided. Among the sons of Eleazar there were sixteen chief men of the house of their fathers, and eight among the sons of Ithamar according to the house of their fathers.
corruption_summary: Ithamar models the faithful, ordered priestly service that God preserves through generations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the dignity of faithful, ordered ministry in the house of God. Ithamar bore no spectacular calling, but he kept the charge committed to him—the burdens, the boards, the reckoning of the tabernacle—and his line was numbered among the appointed courses. Steady obedience in the appointed task is itself a high service before the LORD.

Set beside his elder brothers Nadab and Abihu, who perished for presumption, Ithamar shows that faithfulness in worship is not invention but submission to God’s order. The regulative care of the sanctuary, the lot-ordered courses, the careful stewardship of holy things—all teach that God will be served as He has appointed, and that He preserves a ministry through those who keep His charge.
roots_summary: The name evokes the palm-fringed coast, a fitting note of order and fruitfulness for a steward of the sanctuary.
roots_lines: Ithamar — Hebrew Ithamar, “palm coast” or “land of palms.”
The element tamar means “palm tree.”
He was fourth and youngest of Aaron’s sons.
His line held the high priesthood through Eli for a season.
Eight of the twenty-four priestly courses sprang from his house.
usage: Like Ithamar, the faithful minister keeps the charge committed to his hand.
The Gershonites and Merarites bore the tabernacle under the oversight of Ithamar.
David ordered eight courses of priests from the house of Ithamar.

etymology: From the Hebrew: Nadab, “liberal” or “willing”; Abihu, “he is my father.”
biblical_def: Nadab and Abihu were the two eldest sons of Aaron, set apart with their father and brothers to minister in the priest’s office. They had been granted a great privilege: with Moses and Aaron and the seventy elders they went up the mount, saw the God of Israel, and did eat and drink in His presence. Yet privilege did not breed reverence. Soon after the tabernacle was consecrated and fire from the LORD had consumed the offering, these two sons took each his censer, put fire therein, and laid incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which He commanded them not. The judgment was immediate and terrible: there went out fire from the LORD and devoured them, and they died before the LORD. Moses declared the meaning to Aaron: I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified; and Aaron held his peace. Their bodies were carried out of the camp in their coats by their cousins, and the priests were forbidden to mourn lest wrath fall upon the whole congregation. Some have linked their presumption to wine, for the very next command forbade priests strong drink when they went into the tabernacle. Nadab and Abihu stand forever as the warning of profane worship—men who approached the holy God on their own terms and were consumed.
webster_summary: Aaron’s two eldest sons, who offered strange fire before the LORD and were devoured by fire from His presence.
webster_full: NADAB AND ABIHU, the two eldest sons of Aaron, set apart to the priesthood.
They saw the God of Israel on the mount with Moses and the elders (Exo 24:9).
They offered strange fire before the LORD, which He commanded them not (Lev 10:1).
Fire went out from the LORD and devoured them, and they died.
They died childless, and the priesthood continued through Eleazar and Ithamar (Num 3:4).
scriptures: Lev 10:1
And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein, and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not.
Lev 10:2
And there went out fire from the LORD, and devoured them, and they died before the LORD.
Lev 10:3
Then Moses said unto Aaron, This is it that the LORD spake, saying, I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me, and before all the people I will be glorified. And Aaron held his peace.
Num 3:4

And Nadab and Abihu died before the LORD, when they offered strange fire before the LORD, in the wilderness of Sinai, and they had no children: and Eleazar and Ithamar ministered in the priest’s office in the sight of Aaron their father.
corruption_summary: Nadab and Abihu are the enduring warning against will-worship—approaching God in any way He has not commanded.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the holiness of God and the peril of self-devised worship. Their fire was strange because the LORD commanded it not; they offered what seemed good in their own eyes rather than what God had appointed, and they were consumed. The regulative principle—that God is to be worshipped only as He has prescribed—is written in their ashes.

Their fall confronts the modern appetite for worship shaped by feeling, novelty, and the worshipper’s own preference. God will be sanctified in them that come nigh Him; He is not honored by sincerity in disobedience. The nearer the privilege, the greater the accountability: these men had seen God and yet trifled with His holiness. Reverence, not innovation, befits those who draw near to a consuming fire.
roots_summary: The brothers’ names speak of willingness and fatherhood, in tragic irony to their willful, fatal presumption.
roots_lines: Nadab — Hebrew, “liberal,” “willing,” or “noble.”
Abihu — Hebrew, “he is my father” or “my father is he.”
They were the first and second sons of Aaron by Elisheba.
The “strange fire” was fire and incense not commanded by the LORD.
They died childless, so their line did not continue the priesthood.
usage: Like Nadab and Abihu, those who worship God on their own terms invite His judgment.
The strange fire of Nadab and Abihu stands against every self-devised act of worship.
God was sanctified in Nadab and Abihu, and Aaron held his peace.

etymology: From the Hebrew: Hophni, “pugilist” or “tadpole”; Phinehas, “mouth of brass” or “the Nubian.”
biblical_def: Hophni and Phinehas were the two sons of Eli the priest at Shiloh, themselves serving in the priest’s office, but the Scripture pronounces them sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD. Their wickedness was great in two regards. First, they corrupted the worship of God, despising the offering of the LORD: by their servants they seized the flesh of the sacrifices with a flesh-hook before the fat was burned, and took it raw by force, so that men abhorred the offering of the LORD. Second, they defiled the very door of the tabernacle, lying with the women that assembled there. Their father Eli rebuked them feebly, but honored his sons above God and restrained them not, and so the LORD purposed to slay them. A man of God and then the boy Samuel foretold the doom: that both should die in one day, and the priesthood be torn from Eli’s house. When Israel rashly carried the ark into battle against the Philistines, Hophni and Phinehas went with it; Israel was smitten, the ark was taken, and the two sons died in one day, as it was spoken. The shock of the tidings broke Eli’s neck, and Phinehas’ wife died in travail, naming her child Ichabod—the glory is departed. Hophni and Phinehas stand as the terrible pattern of priests who profane holy things and perish under the judgment of God.
webster_summary: Eli’s wicked sons, priests who despised the LORD’s offering and defiled the tabernacle, and died in one day.
webster_full: HOPHNI AND PHINEHAS, the two sons of Eli, priests at Shiloh.
They were sons of Belial who knew not the LORD (1Sa 2:12).
They despised the offering, seizing the sacrifices by force before the fat was burned.
They lay with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle.
Both died in one day when the Philistines took the ark (1Sa 4:11).
scriptures: Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.
Wherefore the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD: for men abhorred the offering of the LORD.
And this shall be a sign unto thee, that shall come upon thy two sons, on Hophni and Phinehas; in one day they shall die both of them.
And the ark of God was taken; and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were slain.
corruption_summary: Hophni and Phinehas are the byword of corrupt priests who profane God’s worship and bring His judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the awful guilt of those who profane the worship and offerings of God for their own appetites. These men made the sacrifice contemptible and the sanctuary a place of lust, and men abhorred the offering of the LORD because of them. They knew not the LORD though they ministered before Him—a warning that office without grace is damnation, not protection.

Their account also indicts the weak indulgence of Eli, who honored his sons above God and rebuked but never removed them. The judgment fell on the whole house, and the glory departed with the ark. Pastors and parents alike are warned: presumptuous sin in holy things ripens to ruin, and those who despise the LORD shall be lightly esteemed. God will not hold the profaner guiltless.
roots_summary: Their names are of disputed and lowly sense, fitting two priests whose ministry ended in profanation and death.
roots_lines: Hophni — Hebrew, perhaps “pugilist” or “tadpole,” possibly of Egyptian root.
Phinehas — the same name as Aaron’s grandson, “mouth of brass” or “the Nubian.”
Both were sons of Eli, the priest and judge at Shiloh.
Scripture brands them sons of Belial, worthless men who knew not the LORD.
Their death in one day fulfilled the prophecy against Eli’s house.
usage: Like Hophni and Phinehas, priests who profane the offering bring abhorrence upon the worship of God.
The sin of Hophni and Phinehas made men abhor the offering of the LORD.
Both sons of Eli died in one day, as the man of God had foretold.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “fool” or “foolish, senseless.”
biblical_def: Nabal was a very great man of Maon whose possessions lay in Carmel, with three thousand sheep and a thousand goats; but the man was churlish and evil in his doings, and he was of the house of Caleb. His name, which means “fool,” his wife Abigail confessed to be the very truth of him: as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. When David and his men, who had been a wall about Nabal’s shepherds in the wilderness, sent in a day of feasting to ask provision with all courtesy, Nabal railed at the messengers, asking, Who is David? and likening him to a runaway servant, and sent them away empty. David girded on his sword in wrath, swearing to leave not one of Nabal’s house alive. But Abigail, a woman of good understanding, went swiftly with bread and wine and dressed sheep, fell at David’s feet, took the blame upon herself, and pleaded with wisdom that he not shed blood causelessly nor avenge himself. David blessed her counsel and turned back. When Abigail told Nabal in the morning, after his drunken feast, his heart died within him and he became as a stone; and about ten days after, the LORD smote Nabal that he died. So David said, Blessed be the LORD that hath pleaded the cause of my reproach, and kept me from evil. Nabal stands as the scriptural fool—ungrateful, drunken, and proud—struck down by the very God his folly ignored.
webster_summary: The churlish, foolish man of Maon and Carmel, Abigail’s husband, who railed at David and was struck dead by the LORD.
webster_full: NABAL, a very great but churlish man of Maon, with possessions in Carmel.
His name means “fool,” and folly was with him, as his wife confessed (1Sa 25:25).
He railed at David’s messengers and refused them provision (1Sa 25:10).
His wife Abigail’s wisdom turned away David’s sworn vengeance.
The LORD smote Nabal that he died about ten days after his drunken feast (1Sa 25:38).
scriptures: Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb.
And Nabal answered David’s servants, and said, Who is David? and who is the son of Jesse? there be many servants now a days that break away every man from his master.

Let not my lord, I pray thee, regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send.
And it came to pass about ten days after, that the LORD smote Nabal, that he died.
corruption_summary: Nabal is the very portrait of the biblical fool—proud, ungrateful, and senseless toward God and man.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover is the ruin of the fool who lives for himself, despising both the kindness of others and the providence of God. Nabal had been guarded by David’s men, yet he answered favor with insult and feasted like a king while denying a morsel to those who shielded him. The fool says in his heart there is no God, and lives as if he answered to none.

His account also magnifies God’s righteous government and the place of wise counsel. David was about to avenge himself in bloodshed, but Abigail’s prudence stayed his hand, and the LORD Himself smote Nabal—teaching that vengeance is the Lord’s, who will repay. The believer learns to leave his cause with God, and to dread the hardened folly that drinks and presumes until the day it is struck as a stone.
roots_summary: The name is itself a verdict: Nabal means fool, and folly was with him to his death.
roots_lines: Nabal — Hebrew Naval, “fool” or “senseless, vile.”
The same root names the moral fool throughout the Wisdom books.
He dwelt in Maon, with great flocks pastured at Carmel of Judah.
He was of the house of Caleb, yet wholly unlike his faithful forefather.
His wife Abigail, after his death, became one of David’s wives.
usage: Like Nabal, the ungrateful fool answers kindness with insult and reaps the judgment of God.
Abigail confessed that as Nabal’s name was, so was he—folly was with him.
The LORD smote Nabal, vindicating David, who had withheld his own hand from blood.
